title: Protecting people without chilling care
label: 16 November 2026 · Conversion Practices Bill
summary: The committee examined whether the draft Bill would stop abusive conversion practices without deterring parents and health professionals from supporting people who are questioning their gender or sexuality. Baroness Cass and Professor Gillian Leng warned that unclear standards and the threat of complaints or prosecution could make clinicians avoid difficult but necessary conversations. They supported action against abuse but raised concerns about the Bill as drafted. Regulators described the standards and complaint processes they already use, while agreeing that clearer clinical guidance and a more clearly limited healthcare exemption could help.

glossary.definition: Attempts to change or suppress someone's sexual orientation or gender identity.
A provision intended to protect legitimate healthcare from being treated as a criminal conversion practice.
A criminal case brought by a person or organisation rather than by the state prosecution service.
Official guidance that the law requires an organisation to issue.
The Crown Prosecution Service, which decides whether criminal cases in England and Wales should go to court.
The General Medical Council, which sets professional standards for doctors and can investigate concerns about them.
The Care Quality Commission, which inspects and regulates many health and care services in England.
The Health and Care Professions Council, which registers and regulates several health and care professions.
Lists of health or care practitioners checked and approved by the Professional Standards Authority.
The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, which produces guidance on health and care.
A regulator's assessment of whether a professional is safe and suitable to continue working.
A memorandum of understanding: an agreement between organisations about how they will work or act.

chapters.title: Cass's concerns about the draft
chapters.takeaway: Cass supports banning abusive conversion practices, but says this Bill's wording could expose careful care and ordinary family decisions to complaints.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Baroness Cass, you previously welcomed the Bill's principles. Having now read it, do you think its definition is clear enough?

turns.speaker: Baroness Cass
turns.text: No. I welcomed what the Minister had described, but I hadn't seen the Bill when I commented publicly. Having read it, I don't think it's tight enough to prevent serious unintended consequences.

turns.speaker: Baroness Cass
turns.text: The healthcare exemption depends on whether someone acted far below the standards expected of a person in their role. But standards in this field are unclear and disputed, including by people who disagree with my review.

turns.speaker: Baroness Cass
turns.text: A young person may leave a painful conversation upset, perhaps because they didn't get the treatment they wanted, and feel the clinician treated them badly. Some people may use that experience to pursue clinicians who are doing careful, exploratory work.

turns.speaker: Baroness Cass
turns.text: I'm also worried parents could be caught up despite that not being the intention. Not using a child's requested pronouns, or restricting money for a binder or hormones, might be seen as falling within the Bill.

turns.speaker: Lord Isaac
turns.text: Do you still stand by your report's statement that no LGBTQ+ group should be subjected to conversion practices?

turns.speaker: Baroness Cass
turns.text: Absolutely. Those practices are abhorrent. I've spent years trying to find a way to protect people from them without accidentally drawing in people the Bill isn't meant to catch.

turns.speaker: Baroness Brown of Silvertown
turns.text: Do laws in other countries offer a better model?

turns.speaker: Baroness Cass
turns.text: It's too early to tell. The laws are relatively new, there haven't been cases, and I don't know whether they've discouraged people from seeking or providing care.

turns.speaker: Lord Isaac
turns.text: Would your proposed wording about registered practitioners and open-ended therapeutic conversations address the concerns?

turns.speaker: Baroness Cass
turns.text: It was a probing amendment, an attempt to improve the Bill. Clinicians in the new services still fear complaints, and even an investigation can be devastating, whether or not the person is eventually cleared.

turns.speaker: Baroness Cass
turns.text: That fear matters in a field already short of staff. Why take a job where you might face a complaint if you can work elsewhere?

turns.speaker: Lord Isaac
turns.text: But don't your examples still have to meet the Bill's requirements of abuse and serious harm?

turns.speaker: Baroness Cass
turns.text: The question isn't only whether a case would succeed. A person may still report the clinician, setting off a difficult process.

turns.speaker: Baroness Browning
turns.text: Your review said that terms such as 'affirmative' and 'exploratory' therapy have been weaponised. Has reading the Bill changed your concern?

turns.speaker: Baroness Cass
turns.text: No. The debate has become more hostile and polarised. Some people label the exploratory approach in my review as conversion therapy, and there are people on different sides who may use the debate to undermine others.

chapters.title: Parents, young people and difficult conversations
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses said sensitive conversations can cause distress without being abusive, and that lawmakers must weigh protection against the risk of deterring support.

turns.speaker: Olivia Bailey
turns.text: If the Bill clearly protected parents and clinicians from vexatious complaints, would you support a ban on abusive conversion practices?

turns.speaker: Baroness Cass
turns.text: I would need to see the exact wording. One mother told me that her daughter was distressed and identifying as a boy, and that she tried to be supportive while not using the requested name and pronouns.

turns.speaker: Baroness Cass
turns.text: The girl's father reported the mother to social services. At the time the mother spoke to me, an investigation had lasted 11 months and the younger child had stopped attending school and was wetting the bed. I worry someone could make a similar report to police under this Bill.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Would the Bill be improved by requiring official guidance on how it should be applied?

turns.speaker: Baroness Cass
turns.text: Potentially, yes, but I can't yet say how it should be written.

turns.speaker: Professor Leng
turns.text: We need to remember that some people seeking care are distressed and uncertain. Clinicians need to be able to ask open questions and explore what is happening without steering the person towards a particular outcome.

turns.speaker: Professor Leng
turns.text: If the definition is too broad, clinicians may avoid conversations that people need. They may then search online, where abusive practices also happen and may be harder to control.

turns.speaker: Baroness Prentis of Banbury
turns.text: Is your concern that simply passing a law could deter people from providing care, even if the Bill also required guidance?

turns.speaker: Baroness Cass
turns.text: Yes. During my review, people at opposite ends of the debate couldn't be brought into the same room. The hostility has even led one doctor to need security when speaking publicly.

turns.speaker: Baroness Prentis of Banbury
turns.text: Could the Bill also deter people from reporting unsafe practice?

turns.speaker: Baroness Cass
turns.text: That is a concern too. I described a public case involving a GP who raised safety concerns and later left her job; she has brought an employment tribunal case.

turns.speaker: Baroness Brown of Silvertown
turns.text: Could failing to pass a Bill also leave people unprotected?

turns.speaker: Baroness Cass
turns.text: Yes. It's a difficult balance of risks, not a choice between risk and no risk. Gender-questioning young people can have very different needs.

turns.speaker: Baroness Cass
turns.text: Some will remain gender-incongruent into adulthood and may benefit from medical or surgical transition. Others express distress through gender questions, and acting too quickly medically can have a serious cost. For someone with a long-standing trans identity, by contrast, the costs of not being able to live in their identified gender may outweigh treatment risks.

turns.speaker: Danny Beales
turns.text: Are you calling for every healthcare professional to be completely exempt from the Bill?

turns.speaker: Baroness Cass
turns.text: That's one possibility, with drawbacks. Another would be to approve particular centres or organisations. I don't know which is best.

turns.speaker: Naz Shah
turns.text: Should the Bill allow private prosecutions, and do you support it as drafted?

turns.speaker: Baroness Cass
turns.text: Private prosecutions add a risk, especially when it's unclear where the line is. And no, I can't support the Bill in its current form. I support action against conversion practices, but I hadn't read the Bill when I first commented on its principles.

turns.speaker: Professor Leng
turns.text: I think the risk of people not getting the care and support they need may be greater unless there is a broad exemption for regulated healthcare settings. Clear professional guidance and training would also help clinicians defend their decisions.

turns.speaker: Professor Leng
turns.text: I've seen people avoid difficult conversations in other areas of medicine because they fear being drawn into legal trouble. That is why I worry this could happen here too.

chapters.title: What counts as good care?
chapters.takeaway: Cass and Leng said the Bill needs clearer standards, while arguing that a painful or distressing conversation is not automatically abusive.

turns.speaker: Sir Jeremy Wright
turns.text: Is the Bill's final test—whether someone suffers serious harm, alarm or distress—high enough? And is 'abusive' clearly defined?

turns.speaker: Baroness Cass
turns.text: I'm not sure abuse is defined separately from serious harm, alarm or distress. A clinician and young person can experience the same conversation differently, and distress may arise from what it brings up rather than from anything the clinician did wrong.

turns.speaker: Sir Jeremy Wright
turns.text: Would it help if the distress had to be intended, or something the clinician should have foreseen?

turns.speaker: Baroness Cass
turns.text: A conversation can be painful and still be necessary. You can't help someone work through sexual abuse, for example, without discussing it.

turns.speaker: Baroness Cass
turns.text: Some young people who come for help have also experienced serious mental-health difficulties, autism, eating disorders, self-harm or unexplained physical symptoms. Their gender distress may be connected to other difficulties. That's not the same as assuming every young person's identity is temporary.

turns.speaker: Professor Leng
turns.text: These conversations can also be very difficult for parents. We need supportive settings where families and clinicians can speak sensitively, not practices such as aversion therapy or hypnosis, which are plainly unacceptable.

turns.speaker: Baroness Cass
turns.text: One parent described a daughter who later stopped identifying as transgender. At the time, the family was distressed and the young person was self-harming and asking for hormones and surgery. The parent felt that professionals had caused harm, but later believed that her own failure to understand had been protective.

turns.speaker: Baroness Cass
turns.text: That is one family's experience, not a pattern that applies to everyone. Some young people will go on to have a stable trans identity and a successful life.

turns.speaker: Lord Scriven
turns.text: You say standards are unclear and disputed. What standards would clinicians actually be judged against?

turns.speaker: Baroness Cass
turns.text: That's the key question. Some organisations favour a more affirmative approach, though they also call for proper assessment. A multi-professional group is developing training and a framework, but other professional groups may favour different standards.

turns.speaker: Professor Leng
turns.text: A guideline should be developed with different professionals, young people and parents involved. It should guide good practice without requiring every case to be handled identically. If a clinician departs from it, they should explain and record why.

turns.speaker: Lord Scriven
turns.text: Would that apply to both registered and unregistered practitioners?

turns.speaker: Professor Leng
turns.text: It would clearly matter for regulated professionals. Unregulated practice is a wider problem that needs a broader answer.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Would a case under this Bill require a child to give evidence about serious harm?

turns.speaker: Baroness Cass
turns.text: I don't know how a case could be proved without hearing from the child. The Bill also asks courts to consider all the circumstances, and clinicians might be unable to explain their reasoning without revealing confidential family information.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: And a prosecutor would still have to prove the offence to a jury beyond reasonable doubt.

chapters.title: What regulators already do
chapters.takeaway: The regulators reported few complaints about conversion practices and said they already rely on professional standards, service rules and existing powers to act on unsafe care.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The second panel was asked how well current regulation works in gender and sexual-orientation care.

turns.speaker: Mark Swindells
turns.text: The GMC gets relatively few complaints about doctors in this area. We set professional standards, including expectations that doctors explain the risks and benefits of medical treatment.

turns.speaker: Dr Chopra
turns.text: The CQC checks services against rules about safe, respectful, person-centred care and protecting people from abuse. We have acted where gender services fell below those standards, including rating one provider inadequate after finding serious failings.

turns.speaker: Andrew Smith
turns.text: The HCPC sets standards for the conduct and skills of the professionals it registers. We receive very few concerns of this kind and aren't aware of reports about our registrants using conversion practices.

turns.speaker: Naz Shah
turns.text: How can regulators judge reasonable standards in such a disputed field?

turns.speaker: Dr Chopra
turns.text: There are service specifications, professional standards and guidance from colleges and other groups. We use those when inspecting services, alongside the recommendations accepted by NHS England.

turns.speaker: Mark Swindells
turns.text: The medical colleges and NICE are working on guidance across professional groups. At present, clinical guidance is contested, which makes it harder for regulators to know what good practice looks like.

turns.speaker: Lord Scriven
turns.text: Have complaints about this subject been tagged in a way that lets you count them?

turns.speaker: Mark Swindells
turns.text: Not as a separate category. We manually checked cases, though, and are reasonably confident the number is small.

turns.speaker: Baroness Browning
turns.text: Would all your professional standards need to meet the level of clinical negligence to protect people from private prosecution?

turns.speaker: Mark Swindells
turns.text: Our standards describe good practice and support our own regulatory decisions; they're not a test of criminal or civil negligence. We rely on clinical guidance from professional bodies and other organisations.

turns.speaker: Sir Jeremy Wright
turns.text: Should the Bill's healthcare exemption be limited to people and services that are regulated?

turns.speaker: Dr Chopra
turns.text: Yes. The exemption should protect people providing legitimate healthcare, not anyone who claims to be doing something similar. It could cover regulated services and practitioners on approved registers.

turns.speaker: Andrew Smith
turns.text: A clearer limit could stop people with no connection to legitimate healthcare using the exemption, while still protecting clinicians having difficult, evidence-based conversations.

turns.speaker: Mark Swindells
turns.text: We agree. Registration means a person has training, must meet professional standards and can be investigated if concerns arise.

turns.speaker: Sir Jeremy Wright
turns.text: The Bill also covers procedures similar to medical or surgical care even when they're not for a medical condition. Does that create uncertainty?

turns.speaker: Andrew Smith
turns.text: I'm not sure what that wording is intended to catch or exclude.

turns.speaker: Dr Chopra
turns.text: I'm also unsure whether those procedures fall under any regulated service. I'd need to check.

turns.speaker: Baroness Prentis of Banbury
turns.text: Do you know how many therapists in this field aren't regulated?

turns.speaker: Mark Swindells
turns.text: No, we don't hold that information.

turns.speaker: Baroness Prentis of Banbury
turns.text: The CQC regulates England, but the Bill covers England and Wales. Are online providers based overseas another gap?

turns.speaker: Dr Chopra
turns.text: Yes. Some online providers are based abroad and outside our reach. I know of a couple of high-profile examples, but we can't say how widespread it is.

chapters.title: How a criminal case might interact with regulation
chapters.takeaway: The panel said courts and professional regulators use different tests, but unclear standards could leave both prosecutors and clinicians struggling to apply the Bill.

turns.speaker: Lord Isaac
turns.text: You say conversion practices breach your standards already. Would the Bill change how you regulate complaints?

turns.speaker: Andrew Smith
turns.text: We issued guidance in 2022 saying conversion practices aren't acceptable for our registrants. We refer to an agreement between professional bodies, and a new criminal definition wouldn't automatically change how we handle a regulatory complaint.

turns.speaker: Mark Swindells
turns.text: If a doctor were convicted, the GMC wouldn't repeat the criminal case. We have a process that takes account of convictions, and our existing standards already require evidence-based care that isn't shaped by a doctor's personal beliefs.

turns.speaker: Dr Chopra
turns.text: We also regard conversion practices as wrong. Where we have concerns about an individual in a service, we'd share them with the relevant professional regulator and consider whether the service needs inspection.

turns.speaker: Danny Beales
turns.text: Have you seen more vexatious complaints since referring to the agreement on conversion practices?

turns.speaker: Mark Swindells
turns.text: No. We have a policy for handling vexatious complaints, though deciding whether a complaint meets that description requires judgment.

turns.speaker: Andrew Smith
turns.text: We haven't seen an increase on this subject either.

turns.speaker: Dr Chopra
turns.text: Nor have we. The CQC isn't currently a signatory to the agreement, but we could consider it when it is reviewed.

turns.speaker: Danny Beales
turns.text: Can you predict whether the Bill would increase complaints?

turns.speaker: Andrew Smith
turns.text: I can't predict that. The Bill could bring more attention to the subject, but we currently receive very few reports.

turns.speaker: Dr Chopra
turns.text: Some clinicians have told me they fear a rise in complaints, but it's difficult to forecast.

turns.speaker: Mark Swindells
turns.text: I would give the same answer.

turns.speaker: Danny Beales
turns.text: Have you spoken with regulators overseas about similar laws?

turns.speaker: Mark Swindells
turns.text: We've compared laws in about 27 places, but haven't spoken directly with the regulators there.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: If a person reports abuse, would they go to police, and how would a clinician establish that they qualify for the exemption?

turns.speaker: Mark Swindells
turns.text: If a doctor on our register is charged, they should tell us. We would usually let the criminal case proceed rather than start a separate investigation at the same time.

turns.speaker: Lord Scriven
turns.text: Does the Bill make you, as regulators, decide what the criminal law means by conduct far below the required standard?

turns.speaker: Mark Swindells
turns.text: We set professional standards, but a regulator doesn't treat every departure from them as proof that someone is unsafe. The missing piece is agreement on suitable clinical guidance.

turns.speaker: Andrew Smith
turns.text: I read the Bill as allowing the court to consider professional standards alongside other evidence, not as making one regulatory document the sole test.

turns.speaker: Baroness Prentis of Banbury
turns.text: Would regulators give expert evidence about whether a practitioner's actions fell far below the right standard?

turns.speaker: Andrew Smith
turns.text: We could explain our standards and where practitioners should look for guidance. We wouldn't make the clinical judgment for the court.

turns.speaker: Mark Swindells
turns.text: A defendant would more usually have an independent expert. A regulator could explain its standards without taking a side.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: If a person were acquitted, would that end the regulator's involvement?

turns.speaker: Mark Swindells
turns.text: Not necessarily. A criminal court and a regulator assess different things. We may still consider whether the person is safe to practise in future.

turns.speaker: Andrew Smith
turns.text: We could also take regulatory action after a failed prosecution, because our assessment isn't limited to whether the criminal offence was proved.

turns.speaker: Dr Chopra
turns.text: As a service regulator, we'd share concerns with the appropriate professional body and consider whether the provider itself needs attention.

turns.speaker: Baroness Browning
turns.text: Could you clarify how the physiotherapy body's withdrawal from the agreement over its application to children affects your approach?

turns.speaker: Andrew Smith
turns.text: I don't know enough about that decision to answer now, but I'll look into it and write to the committee.
